title: A run-state conflict still kills the run (FETCH_HEAD half fixed in ea1baed)
description:
ROOT CAUSE of both silent run deaths in the pwp production run on 2026-09-14.

internal/reconcile/reconcile.go:1140-1150 (checkpoint). On a conflict the code does exactly the right recovery — it re-fetches, re-reads the checkpoint, and adopts the newer sequence and tick states — and then returns an error anyway. The error propagates out of the run loop and the process exits. It does all the work to recover and then quits.

The conflict is not exotic. It is produced by a NORMAL, DOCUMENTED operator action: `ticfac finding <epic> <key> --promote-as ...` writes a decision to the run's own integration branch. Triaging a finding while the run is going is not a misuse — a tick with an untriaged finding cannot close, so the operator is REQUIRED to triage during the run. The tool's two supported activities race each other, and the run loses.

Evidence, both deaths:
- 20:40:55 operator promoted finding 6e652f26 (3r2) -> run died at 20:42:16, between tier_derived for gms and its claim. No log was captured, cause unknown at the time.
- 21:09 operator promoted finding 392e2988 (gms) -> run died at 21:12:57, immediately after closing gms, before dispatching sx5. Captured: `reconcile: the run state moved under this reconciler while writing running: conflict_exists`.

Both deaths were silent to the feed: the last feed line is an ordinary success, so a feed subscriber cannot distinguish 'finished this tick' from 'died'.

Required:
- A CAS conflict on the run state is a NORMAL condition, not a fatal one. After the re-fetch that already happens, continue the loop against the refreshed state. Bound it: fail only after N consecutive conflicts on the same write, the way integrate.go and refresh.go already bound their branch-moved retries.
- The feed must carry a terminal line when the run dies for any reason, so silence never has to be interpreted.

Acceptance: a test writes a competing decision to the run branch mid-run (the shape ticfac finding produces) and asserts the run continues and completes the epic; a second test asserts N consecutive conflicts on one write still fail, and that the failure emits a terminal feed line.
notes:
2026-09-14 23:15 - CORRECTION to the description's causal claim, made after checking the commit timeline on origin/epic/pwp.

The description asserts that the operator's `ticfac finding --promote-as` caused both deaths. That is NOT established. The timeline for death 2 contradicts the simple version:

  23:09:24  ticfac  update .ticfac/runs/epic-pwp/findings/392e2988....json   <- the operator's triage
  23:10:41  ticfac  create evidence/gate-gms-8-go.json
  23:12:26  ticfac  create evidence/gate-gms-8-pi-runner.json
  23:12:34  ticfac  update checkpoint.json                                   <- a checkpoint write that SUCCEEDED after the triage
  23:12:43  ticfac  note gms
  23:12:54  ticfac  close gms
  ~23:12:57         died: 'the run state moved under this reconciler while writing running: conflict_exists'

A checkpoint write succeeded 3 minutes after the triage, so an unresolved branch advance from that triage is not a sufficient explanation. The writes immediately before the fatal one are the run's OWN tracker publishes (note gms, close gms).

What IS established and is what this tick is for:
1. The fatal error text, captured verbatim from the run log.
2. reconcile.go checkpoint() performs the full recovery on a conflict (Fetch, re-read, adopt sequence and ticks) and then returns an error regardless, so ANY conflict ends the run. That is the defect, independent of what produced the conflict.
3. Both deaths were invisible in the feed: the last line is an ordinary success.

Still open, and the first thing the implementer must settle by REPRODUCING rather than reasoning: what actually advances the state under the reconciler. Leading candidate is that `ticfac finding` and `ticfac findings` construct their own Reconciler against the same run, so a second reconciler is live while the run is going. Do not build the repair on the description's claim without proving it at the base commit first.
2026-09-14 23:19 - ROOT CAUSE FOUND AND REPRODUCED. Supersedes both the description's claim and the previous correction note.

internal/runstate/store.go peek():

    s.git.run("fetch", s.remote, s.branch)
    head = s.git.run("rev-parse", "FETCH_HEAD")
    view = s.git.lsTree(head, Root)

FETCH_HEAD is ONE FILE in .git, shared by every process using that checkout. Any concurrent `git fetch` in the same repository overwrites it. The run then resolves FETCH_HEAD to whatever the OTHER fetch last wrote — typically main — and builds its view by ls-tree of that commit. main has no .ticfac tree, so the view comes back EMPTY.

The failure chain from there:
1. view empty -> Store.Checkpoint() reports exists=false
2. PutCheckpoint takes the CREATE path (CreateIfAbsent) instead of UpdateIfSHA
3. the push is refused (the branch ref moved)
4. peek() re-reads, finds checkpoint.json DOES exist on origin
5. put() returns ConflictExists
6. checkpoint() returns an error and the run exits

This is the only story that explains the exact outcome we captured. ConflictExists is reachable ONLY from the create path; a genuine concurrent checkpoint write by another reconciler would have produced ConflictStaleSHA.

REPRODUCTION (scratch repo, no ticfac needed):
  git fetch origin epic; git rev-parse FETCH_HEAD   -> epic head, view has .ticfac
  git fetch origin      ; git rev-parse FETCH_HEAD   -> main head, view is EMPTY
Confirmed 2026-09-14.

The trigger in both pwp deaths was my own watcher running `git -C <the run's checkout> fetch -q origin` every 15-25 seconds. But the defect is not the watcher. ANY concurrent fetch does this: an operator running git fetch, an editor's auto-fetch, a second tk command, a status script. ticfac tells operators to watch runs and then dies when they do.

SEVERITY IS HIGHER THAN A CRASH. s.head is also set from the clobbered FETCH_HEAD, so a writer can end up building a commit on the WRONG BASE. A crash is the good outcome; a write rooted at main's tree is the bad one. Check every use of s.head for that exposure.

FIX: never read FETCH_HEAD. Fetch into a private per-run ref and read that:
    git fetch --no-write-fetch-head origin +<branch>:refs/ticfac/peek/<run-id>
    git rev-parse refs/ticfac/peek/<run-id>
A private ref is process-local state that no other git command touches. --no-write-fetch-head (git 2.29+) additionally stops ticfac from clobbering FETCH_HEAD for everyone else.

ACCEPTANCE: a test runs a plain `git fetch <remote>` against the run's checkout between two run-state writes and asserts the run continues and the epic completes; a second test asserts peek() resolves its head from the private ref and not from FETCH_HEAD.
2026-09-15 02:34 - AUDIT of the FETCH_HEAD exposure. There are TWO readers, not one, and the second is worse than the first.

  internal/runstate/store.go:280   peek()                  — the run-state store
  internal/reconcile/tracker.go:108 trackerTree.originHead() — the tracker publisher

store.go is the crash we captured. tracker.go is the corruption path:

trackerTree.sync() calls originHead() and then MOVES THE TRACKER WORKTREE to that commit, and leases against it. Clobber FETCH_HEAD with main's head and sync() walks the tracker worktree onto main. Everything tk then reads and writes — claims, notes, closes — is resolved against the wrong tree, and the lease is taken against the wrong base. sync() refuses to move over UNCOMMITTED records, which is a real guard, but a clean worktree moves silently and that is the normal state between publishes.

So the severity ordering is: the run dying is the benign symptom; a tracker publish landing on the wrong base is the harm. Both come from the same line of code shape.

Fix BOTH readers the same way — fetch into a private per-run ref and resolve that, never FETCH_HEAD:
    git fetch --no-write-fetch-head <remote> +<branch>:refs/ticfac/peek/<run-id>
    git rev-parse refs/ticfac/peek/<run-id>

Also add a grep-level guard test: no production file in this repository may read FETCH_HEAD. It is process-global state in a tool that explicitly supports an operator watching a live run, and a reviewer cannot be expected to catch the third occurrence.
2026-09-15 08:18 - STATUS: the root cause is FIXED and committed as ea1baed. What remains open here is the SECOND, independent defect.

FIXED — both FETCH_HEAD readers now fetch into a private per-run ref with --no-write-fetch-head (internal/runstate/store.go peek, internal/reconcile/tracker.go originHead), and a guard test fails if any production file names FETCH_HEAD again. runstate and reconcile suites pass. Verified in production afterwards: the run stayed alive through repeated operator reads of the branch that killed the previous binary three times.

STILL OPEN — checkpoint() in reconcile.go performs the full recovery on a conflict (Fetch, re-read, adopt sequence and ticks) and then returns an error regardless, so ANY conflict still ends the run. FETCH_HEAD was what produced the conflicts we saw; it is not the only thing that can. A second reconciler, a slow push, an operator write between two checkpoints — each is a legitimate conflict the run should absorb by continuing against the refreshed state, bounded by a consecutive-failure count the way integrate.go and refresh.go bound theirs.

Also still open from the original description: every run death should emit a terminal feed line. Both deaths were invisible — the last feed line each time was an ordinary success, so a subscriber could not tell 'finished this tick' from 'died'.
2026-09-15 10:48 - FIXED BY HAND, and the fix found its own gap first.

1. The recover-then-fail half of this tick is NOT a defect, verified rather than assumed. After the FETCH_HEAD fix, the store already absorbs every write to another path (cas_test.go TestAConcurrentWriteToAnotherPathIsNotAConflict, TestAnUpdateIsNotStaleWhenAnotherPathMovedTheRef) — finding triage, decisions, and the run's own tracker publishes. The only conflict that can still reach checkpoint() is a genuine second writer of the checkpoint, and exiting there is the designed guard against two reconcilers. Continuing would overwrite the other writer's progress. So checkpoint() is unchanged.

2. The end-to-end regression test, TestAnOperatorFetchingInTheRunsCheckoutEndsNothing, was written to prove ea1baed. It did not pass on ea1baed. It failed with:
     error: cannot lock ref 'refs/remotes/origin/epic/qeu': is at ab2396a but expected d3513df
   Fetching a branch from a NAMED remote also updates refs/remotes/<remote>/<branch> opportunistically, and an operator's 'git fetch origin' updates the same ref. The two race on its lock and the loser exits 1. The private ref had moved ticfac off FETCH_HEAD and not off shared state. A new death, same trigger.
   Fix: --refmap= (empty) on every production fetch, so only the command-line refspec is updated. Applied to all THREE fetches, including internal/reconcile/git.go:155, which had neither --refmap= nor --no-write-fetch-head and was missed last time.

3. Getting the test to reproduce took two corrections, both worth knowing: the test clone must be ON MAIN, because 'git fetch origin' lists the current branch's upstream first in FETCH_HEAD; and there must be a SECOND WRITER, because a store that is never refused never re-reads origin. Production had both.

Guards: TestNoProductionCodeReadsFetchHead, plus TestEveryProductionFetchStaysOffSharedRefs, which fails naming file:line when a fetch lacks either flag (verified by removing --refmap= from git.go:162). The concurrency test passes 5/5 on the fix.
acceptance_criteria: A competing write to the run branch during a run (as ticfac finding produces) does not end the run: a test drives that race and asserts the epic still completes; repeated conflicts on one write still fail, and every run death emits a terminal feed event
